motion: Can historians prove that Jesus rose from the dead?

sections.title: Historical Method and Public Standards
sections.fourthRowRationale: No fourth row is used; the section contains three pro moves and two con moves.

sections.fourthRowRationale: No fourth row is used; the section contains two pro moves and three con moves.

routes.speaker: Michael Licona
routes.position: Historians can establish Jesus's bodily resurrection with reasonable certainty because it is the best explanation of agreed historical facts.

bridges.statement: The resurrection hypothesis can be established with enough historical probability to answer the motion affirmatively.
Historical hypotheses should be compared by explanatory scope, explanatory power, and avoidance of unsupported additions.
Jesus's crucifixion, the disciples' claimed appearances, and Paul's claimed appearance provide a sufficiently secure factual basis.
Natural or visionary alternatives explain the agreed facts less adequately than bodily resurrection.
The case can rely on widely granted facts without requiring complete Gospel reliability or scriptural inspiration.

routes.speaker: Bart Ehrman
routes.position: Historical methods cannot prove a resurrection because they establish probable events from public evidence, whereas resurrection remains an extraordinary theological explanation.

bridges.statement: Historical evidence cannot establish Jesus's resurrection as having probably occurred.
A method confined to probable historical explanations cannot establish a miracle defined by extraordinary improbability.
The late, non-eyewitness, dependent, and inconsistent resurrection traditions do not supply the source quality historians seek.
Postmortem visionary experiences provide a recurrent historical explanation for the appearance claims without requiring resurrection.
A historical conclusion must rest on evidence and assumptions available across theological viewpoints.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: established with reasonable or adequate certainty
historians talk in terms of probability
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Historical proof means establishing a conclusion with reasonable or adequate certainty, not eliminating every possible doubt.
moves.inventoryRationale: This definition fixes the evidential threshold Licona must meet throughout his affirmative case.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the more criteria that are solidly met by hypothesis
the greater the probability it has of being accurate
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: The probability of a historical hypothesis rises as it satisfies explanatory criteria more fully.
moves.inventoryRationale: This supplies the inferential rule connecting comparative explanatory performance to historical probability.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: three facts pertaining to the resurrection of jesus
jesus death by crucifixion
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Jesus's crucifixion and the disciples' belief that the risen Jesus appeared to them belong to the proposed historical bedrock.
moves.inventoryRationale: These are two of the principal facts the resurrection hypothesis is offered to explain.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: paul the persecutor of the christian church converted to christianity
the risen jesus appearing to him
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Paul's conversion after an experience he understood as an appearance of the risen Jesus is a distinct bedrock fact.
moves.inventoryRationale: Paul's prior opposition is used to broaden the explanatory burden beyond experiences among Jesus's followers.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's a stretch that claimed that the early christians would have used this text
their experiences had convinced them
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Scriptural reflection alone is unlikely to have generated bodily-resurrection belief unless appearance experiences had already convinced the disciples.
moves.inventoryRationale: This challenges Licona's selected wishful-thinking alternative at its account of how bodily-resurrection belief arose.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it accounts for jesus death by crucifixion
it explains all three facts without a bit of strain
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: The resurrection hypothesis directly explains the crucifixion, the disciples' appearances, and Paul's appearance without strain.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Licona's central application of explanatory scope and power to the resurrection hypothesis.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: it's the best explanation of the known facts
yes historians can prove that jesus rose from the dead
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies at the conclusion of Licona's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Because resurrection substantially outperforms competing explanations of the known facts, historians may hold it as quite to very probable.
moves.inventoryRationale: This explicitly completes Licona's route from explanatory comparison to the affirmative answer.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: independent multiple sources to be consistent with one another
if they contradict one another then you've got a problem
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Historians prefer independent sources that remain mutually consistent, since contradictions undermine confidence about which account to rely upon.
moves.inventoryRationale: This establishes a source-evaluation standard later applied to the Gospel narratives.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: they are not contemporary accounts
these accounts are not written by eyewitnesses
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: The Gospels are separated from Jesus's death by decades, are not eyewitness accounts, and do not internally claim their traditional authorship.
moves.inventoryRationale: This directly challenges the temporal proximity and eyewitness status of the resurrection sources.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: one kid tells a story to the next kid
it's a different story
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's opening phase identified in README.md.
moves.proposition: Repeated oral transmission predictably changes stories before they are written down.
moves.inventoryRationale: This provides Ehrman's mechanism for the development of divergent resurrection traditions.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: historians can only establish what probably happened
miracles in any given instance are the least probable occurrence
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's opening phase identified in README.md and explicitly contrasts his probability rule with Licona's account.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman argues that historical method seeks probable events while miracles are extraordinary departures from the natural order and thus begin as the least probable occurrences.

moves.proposition: Historical method establishes probable events, whereas miracles are by definition spectacularly unusual and least probable.
moves.inventoryRationale: This states Ehrman's main methodological barrier to historical proof of resurrection.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how can the least probable occurrence a miracle ever be the most probable
you can't use historical evidence to prove it
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's opening phase identified in README.md and directly rejects Licona's affirmative conclusion.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman contends that an event classified as least probable cannot become the most probable historical conclusion, even if its occurrence remains logically possible.

moves.proposition: Historians cannot prove resurrection because their discipline cannot establish its least probable explanation as the most probable occurrence.
moves.inventoryRationale: This converts Ehrman's probability premise into his explicit negative answer to the motion.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: i did not build my case for the resurrection this evening on biblical inerrancy
only those facts that were virtually indisputed by historians
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's first rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Licona answers that his case does not depend on Gospel authorship, dating, complete trustworthiness, or biblical inerrancy.
He restricts his case to facts he says historians widely grant despite broader transmission concerns.

moves.proposition: Licona's argument relies on widely granted facts rather than biblical inerrancy, traditional authorship, or comprehensive Gospel reliability.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is his principal answer to Ehrman's source-wide reliability challenge.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: some of jesus followers came to believe that he had been raised from the dead
there is no doubt that paul believed
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's first rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Licona cites Ehrman's own acceptance that followers claimed appearances and that Paul believed he saw the risen Jesus, arguing these facts survive the source criticism.

moves.proposition: Ehrman's own stated conclusions grant the disciples' resurrection belief and Paul's claimed appearance, preserving Licona's factual base.
moves.inventoryRationale: The reply uses the opponent's concessions to defend the core data despite disputed Gospel reliability.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the greatest explanatory scope power and less ad hoc
the best explanation the most probable explanation
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's first rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Licona maintains that the hypothesis best satisfying historical explanatory criteria should be accepted as most probable before considering further theological implications.

moves.proposition: If resurrection best satisfies historical explanatory criteria, it may be accepted as the probable historical conclusion independently of further theological inference.
moves.inventoryRationale: This defends the legitimacy of reaching resurrection through historical comparison rather than excluding it categorically.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: how exactly does the crucifixion of jesus provide evidence
there were thousands of people who were crucified
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's first rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman distinguishes a necessary precondition for resurrection from evidence favoring resurrection, noting that many crucifixions did not imply resurrections.

moves.proposition: Jesus's crucifixion is a necessary precondition for resurrection but is not itself positive evidence that resurrection occurred.
moves.inventoryRationale: This directly contests the evidential relevance of the first proposed bedrock fact.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: somebody claimed they saw him alive afterwards
rock solid evidence that apollonius of tiana was raised from the dead
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's first rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman argues that treating postmortem appearance claims as sufficient resurrection evidence would also support resurrection claims about Apollonius and other ancient figures.

moves.proposition: Appearance claims alone cannot establish resurrection without also validating comparable postmortem claims about other ancient figures.
moves.inventoryRationale: The comparison tests whether Licona's proposed evidence discriminates resurrection from parallel claims.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: a real tangible experience with him
experiences that happened multiple times throughout history
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's first rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman agrees that experiences drove belief but proposes tangible postmortem visions rather than bodily resurrection as their cause.
He argues that recurrent experiences of deceased loved ones supply a historically familiar rival explanation for the appearance data.

moves.proposition: The disciples could have had vivid, tangible postmortem experiences like recurrent experiences reported by bereaved people without Jesus bodily returning to life.
moves.inventoryRationale: This gives the principal natural historical alternative to the resurrection hypothesis.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: miracles must be least probable by natural causes
if god exists and wanted to raise jesus
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's second rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Licona grants that resurrection is improbable through natural causes but argues that this does not determine its probability under intentional divine causation.
He contends that if God exists and intended the event, resurrection need not remain the least probable explanation.

moves.proposition: Resurrection's improbability under natural causes does not establish its overall improbability if an existing God intended to raise Jesus.
moves.inventoryRationale: This directly contests the premise supporting Ehrman's categorical probability barrier.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: apollonius fails in every single one of these categories
the earliest account that we have 125 years after the death of apollonius
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's second rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Licona distinguishes Apollonius by alleging a much later surviving account and the absence of comparable multiple sources.

moves.proposition: The Apollonius parallel is evidentially weaker because its surviving account is much later and lacks comparable multiple-source support.
moves.inventoryRationale: This answers the parity challenge by comparing the historical quality of the respective source bases.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
quoteEligibleExactSpans: in no case do these people go back and check the person's tomb
they don't think that it's a bodily resurrected
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Licona's second rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Licona accepts apparitions but distinguishes them from claims involving an emptied tomb and a transformed corpse.

moves.proposition: Ordinary postmortem apparitions do not normally produce a checked-tomb claim or belief in the bodily resurrection of a transformed corpse.
moves.inventoryRationale: This attempts to show that Ehrman's recurrent apparition class does not explain the specific bodily content of the resurrection belief.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: does that show anything about the truth claims of islam
paul did convert from being an enemy to being a friend
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's second rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman argues that movement from hostility to adherence occurs in other religions and does not establish a miracle's truth.
He preserves the distinction between conceding Paul's conversion and conceding that Paul's interpretation was historically correct.

moves.proposition: Paul's conversion from opponent to adherent establishes his changed conviction, not the truth of a miraculous cause.
moves.inventoryRationale: This directly attacks the extra evidential force Licona assigns to Paul's prior hostility.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: with apollonius we have late sources they are not eyewitnesses and they are biased
now it's either relevant or it's not relevant
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's second rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman argues that Licona cannot call source lateness, bias, and non-eyewitness status irrelevant to Jesus while using them against a parallel claim.
He demands consistent application of the source-quality criteria across the Jesus and Apollonius cases.

moves.proposition: Lateness, bias, and lack of eyewitness testimony must be applied consistently to both Gospel and Apollonius sources.
moves.inventoryRationale: This identifies a direct methodological conflict in Licona's treatment of source quality.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
quoteEligibleExactSpans: the evidence they induce has to be available to everybody
if the historical conclusion requires a theological point of view
moves.attributionBasis: The span lies within Ehrman's second rebuttal phase identified in README.md.

responseComponents.text: Ehrman argues that a conclusion counts as historical only when its evidence and governing assumptions are available across religious viewpoints.
He maintains that dependence on a particular view of God or divine intention makes the resulting conclusion theological rather than historical.

moves.proposition: A conclusion requiring a particular theological viewpoint is not a historical conclusion because historical evidence must be publicly available across viewpoints.
moves.inventoryRationale: This is Ehrman's final methodological answer to Licona's attempt to admit divine causation into historical probability.
